claim: V1, LM, and PM are at distinct hierarchical levels in mouse visual cortex, with V1 at the bottom, LM at an intermediate level, and PM at the top.
source: Pairwise comparisons of average DRs of projections from each of V1, LM, and PM to the other areas showed significant (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U test) differences, demonstrating that V1, LM and PM are at distinct hierarchical levels, with LM at the intermediate level between V1 and PM (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p<0.001) of density ratios of axonal terminations in different layers, which is experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Feedforward projections from V1 have higher L2-4:L1 density ratios (>2.52 ± 0.31) than feedback projections to V1 (<0.72 ± 0.08).
source: The matrix showed that the average DRs in all targets of V1 were >2.52 ± 0.31, whereas the DRs for projections to V1 were <0.72 ± 0.08 (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative measurements of axonal projection density ratios shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Feedforward projections from lower areas avoid L1 and selectively target L2-4.
source: Although most projections involved L1-6, inputs from V1 consistently showed dense terminations in L2-4 of each of the higher areas with much sparser projections in L1.
evidence: The claim is supported by optical density measurements of axonal projections shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Feedback projections from higher areas strongly target L1.
source: In contrast, projections from both LM and PM strongly targeted L1 of V1 while weakly targeting L2-4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The selective targeting of L1 by feedback projections is consistent with observations in other species.
source: The selective targeting of L1 by FB projections is consistent with observations in other species (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Coogan and Burkhalter, 1993; Rockland and Virga, 1989; Henry et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in other species.

claim: PV interneurons have a high connection probability with neighboring pyramidal cells in L2/3 (84.6%) and L5 (46.6%).
source: Recordings from PV and Pyr neurons within ~100 µm of each other resulted in 11/13 (84.6%) and 7/15 (46.6%) synaptically connected pairs in L2/3 and L5, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2g).
evidence: The claim is based on paired electrophysiological recordings data.

claim: Increasing the firing of PV cells results in larger inhibitory postsynaptic currents in connected pyramidal cells.
source: In both layers, increasing the firing of PV cells resulted in larger IPSCs in Pyr cells (n = 11 pairs in L2/3, 7 pairs in L5; Figure 2—figure supplement 2d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing dose-dependent responses.

claim: In the L2/3 FFV1→PM pathway, excitatory input to PV cells is 12.85 ± 4.48-fold stronger than to neighboring pyramidal cells.
source: The mean total current in PV cells was 12.85 ± 4.48-fold stronger than that in neighboring Pyr cells (p<0.001, n = 14 pairs).
evidence: The claim is based on sCRACM measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The time to peak of EPSCs is significantly shorter in PV cells than in pyramidal cells in the FFV1→PM pathway.
source: Similar to observations in thalamocortical and local circuits, the time to peak of EPSCs was significantly shorter in PV than in Pyr cells (Figure 2g; n = 14 pairs, p<0.05, paired t-test), consistent with the notion that PV interneurons can be recruited more rapidly than Pyr neurons in diverse brain areas (Hull et al., 2009; Povysheva et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements and citations to previous studies.

claim: In the FBPM→V1 pathway, excitation of PV cells is only 1.93 ± 0.44-fold stronger than pyramidal cell excitation.
source: In contrast to the FFV1→PM pathway, however, the excitation of PV cells in the FBPM→V1 pathway was only 1.93 ± 0.44-fold stronger than Pyr cell excitation.
evidence: The claim is based on sCRACM measurements comparing feedback and feedforward pathways.

claim: The excitation of PV cells relative to pyramidal cells is weaker in the FBPM→V1 pathway than in the FFV1→PM pathway.
source: Thus, the excitation of PV cells, relative to that of neighboring Pyr cells, was weaker in the FBPM→V1 than in the FFV1→PM pathway (Figure 3g; n = 14 pairs for FFV1→PM, n = 21 pairs for FBPM→V1; p<0.001), similar to previous observations in the L2/3 FFV1→LM and FBLM→V1 pathways (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of electrophysiological data and citation to previous work.

claim: In the FFV1→PM pathway, PV cells exhibit larger EPSCs per pixel than pyramidal cells.
source: In the FFV1→PM pathway, PV cells exhibited larger EPSCs per pixel than Pyr cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) as well as received input over a larger area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of sCRACM data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In the FBPM→V1 pathway, the mean EPSC per pixel between PV and pyramidal cells is not significantly different.
source: In contrast, in the FBPM→V1 pathway, the mean EPSC per pixel between the two cell types were not significantly different (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), indicating that the larger total EPSCs in PV cells were the result of PV cells receiving excitatory input over a larger area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of sCRACM data.

claim: The proportion of inputs to L1 is larger in the FBPM→V1 pathway than in the FFV1→PM pathway for both PV and pyramidal cells.
source: Consistent with the distribution of projections (Figure 1b) the proportion of inputs to L1, relative to total EPSCs, was larger in the FBPM→ V1 pathway than in the FFV1→PM pathway (Figure 3i; p<0.01 for both PV and Pyr cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of laminar input distribution with statistical significance.

claim: In the FFLM→PM pathway, the mean total current in PV cells is 3.62 ± 0.75-fold larger than in neighboring pyramidal cells.
source: In the FFLM→PM pathway, the mean total current in PV cells was 3.62 ± 0.75-fold larger than in neighboring Pyr cells (n = 15 pairs, p<0.02; Figure 4c,g).
evidence: The claim is based on sCRACM measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: In the FBPM→LM pathway, the mean total EPSC to PV cells is 3.77 ± 0.81-fold the total EPSC in neighboring pyramidal cells.
source: In the FBPM→LM pathway, the mean total EPSC to PV cells was 3.77 ± 0.81-fold the total EPSC in neighboring Pyr cells, with substantial input into L1 (n = 18 pairs, p<0.01; Figure 4d–f,h,i; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on sCRACM measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: EPSCs are faster in PV cells than in pyramidal cells in both FFLM→PM and FBPM→LM pathways.
source: Similar to connections between V1 and PM, EPSCs were faster in PV than in Pyr cells in both FFLM→PM and FBPM→LM pathways (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological measurements of EPSC kinetics.

claim: The faster activation of PV cells appears to be a general rule for feedforward inhibition provided by long-range connections.
source: Hence, the faster activation of PV cells appears to be a general rule for FFI provided by long-range connections (Hull et al., 2009; Povysheva et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on observations across multiple pathways and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PV cell excitation normalized to pyramidal cell excitation is stronger in the FFV1→PM pathway than in the FFLM→PM pathway.
source: While PV cells received stronger excitatory inputs than Pyr cells in all four L2/3 pathways described here, the difference in the relative excitation of PV and Pyr was bigger in the FFV1→PM originating at the bottom and terminating at the top of the hierarchy than in the FFLM→PM pathway originating from the higher area, LM (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis of sCRACM data across pathways.

claim: In the FBPM→V1 pathway, the difference in PV/Pyr excitation is smaller than for terminations at an intermediate level in LM.
source: In contrast, in the FBPM→V1 pathway, the difference was smaller for connections originating at the top and terminating at the bottom of the hierarchy than for terminations at an intermediate level in LM (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis of sCRACM data across pathways.

claim: There is a significant decrease in EPSCPV/EPSCPyr ratios when pathways are ordered by hierarchical distance from most feedforward to most feedback.
source: These relationships are evident in a significant (p<0.001, Kruskal-Wallis test) decrease of the EPSCPV/EPSCPyr ratios, when pathways are ordered by hierarchical distance from the most feedforward to the most feedback (Figures 1e, 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data across multiple pathways.

claim: In L5, EPSCs recorded in PV and pyramidal cells upon stimulation of FFV1→PM and FFLM→PM axons are not significantly different.
source: Unlike in L2/3, the EPSCs recorded in L5 PV and Pyr cells upon stimulation of FFV1→PM and FFLM→PM axons were not significantly different (Figure 5a–f).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological measurements in L5 neurons.

claim: The relative excitation of L5 PV cells is smaller than that observed in L2/3 for both feedforward pathways.
source: The relative excitation of L5 PV cells, expressed by the EPSCPV/EPSCPyr ratio, was smaller than that observed in L2/3 for both FF pathways (Figure 5g,h).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis of sCRACM data between layers.

claim: L5 pyramidal cells in PM receive feedforward input at different locations of their dendritic arbor depending on the source.
source: Thus depending on the source of long-range synaptic input, L5 Pyr cells in PM receive FF input at different locations of their dendritic arbor.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of laminar distribution of inputs shown in Figure 5i,j.

claim: L5 pyramidal cells in FFLM→PM exhibit large EPSCs at apical dendrites in L2-4, hundreds of microns distal to the cell body.
source: In particular, L5 Pyr cells in FFLM→PM exhibited large EPSCs at apical dendrites in L2-4, hundreds of microns distal to the cell body (Figure 5d,e,i,j).
evidence: The claim is based on sCRACM mapping data showing spatial distribution of inputs.

claim: The proportion of L2-4 inputs to total EPSC is higher in FFLM→PM than in FFV1→PM for L5 pyramidal cells but not for PV cells.
source: The proportion of such L2-4 inputs to the total EPSC was higher in FFLM→PM than in FFV1→PM for L5 Pyr cells but not for PV cells, whose input distributions were similar in both pathways (Figure 5i,j).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of laminar input distribution.

claim: Activation of FBPM→V1 or FBPM→LM projecting axons results in EPSCs of similar magnitudes in neighboring PV and pyramidal cells in L5.
source: Activation of either FBPM→V1 or the FBPM→LM projecting axons resulted in EPSCs of similar magnitudes in neighboring PV and Pyr cells (Figure 6a–f), with the strongest inputs primarily recorded at proximal dendrites in L5 for both cell types (Figure 6g).
evidence: The claim is based on sCRACM measurements in L5 feedback pathways.

claim: The stronger activation of PV cells observed in L2/3 is absent in L5.
source: These results suggest that the stronger activation of PV cells observed in L2/3 is absent in L5.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of L2/3 and L5 data showing no significant differences in L5.

claim: There is no significant difference between EPSCPV/EPSCPyr ratios for L5 cell pairs across different pathways.
source: Consistent with this observation, we found no significant difference between the EPSCPV/EPSCPyr ratios for L5 cell pairs for the different pathways (Figure 6h), suggesting equal potency of FFI among these pathways regardless of whether they are FF or FB.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis showing no significant differences (p>0.2, Kruskal-Wallis test).

claim: EPSCs in PV cells show faster rise times than those in pyramidal cells in all L5 pathways.
source: Similar to L2/3, however, the EPSCs in PV cells showed faster rise times than those in Pyr cells in all L5 pathways (Figure 6i).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological measurements of EPSC kinetics.

claim: Interareal gain control depends on the hierarchical position of the source and target areas.
source: Our results indicate that interareal gain control depends on the hierarchical position of the source and the target, the direction of information flow through the network, and the laminar location of target neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings across multiple pathways.

claim: Interareal gain control depends on the direction of information flow through the network.
source: Our results indicate that interareal gain control depends on the hierarchical position of the source and the target, the direction of information flow through the network, and the laminar location of target neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings comparing feedforward and feedback pathways.

claim: Interareal gain control depends on the laminar location of target neurons.
source: Our results indicate that interareal gain control depends on the hierarchical position of the source and the target, the direction of information flow through the network, and the laminar location of target neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings comparing L2/3 and L5.

claim: Interareal excitation is stronger in PV neurons than in pyramidal neurons in all layer 2/3 pathways.
source: While interareal excitation was stronger in PV than in pyramidal neurons in all layer 2/3 pathways, we observed a gradual scaling down of the inhibition/excitation ratio from the most feedforward to the most feedback pathway.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings across all L2/3 pathways examined.

claim: There is a gradual scaling down of the inhibition/excitation ratio from the most feedforward to the most feedback pathway in L2/3.
source: While interareal excitation was stronger in PV than in pyramidal neurons in all layer 2/3 pathways, we observed a gradual scaling down of the inhibition/excitation ratio from the most feedforward to the most feedback pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis showing a significant trend across pathways (p<0.001).

claim: Most interareal feedforward and feedback connections synapse onto PV-expressing fast-spiking interneurons.
source: Although interareal FF and FB connections terminate on multiple types of GABAergic neurons, most of them synapse onto PV-expressing fast-spiking interneurons (Gonchar and Burkhalter, 1999; Gonchar and Burkhalter, 2003; Hangya et al., 2014), which provide feedforward inhibition (FFI) to local Pyr cells (Dong et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: PV interneurons provide feedforward inhibition to local pyramidal cells.
source: Although interareal FF and FB connections terminate on multiple types of GABAergic neurons, most of them synapse onto PV-expressing fast-spiking interneurons (Gonchar and Burkhalter, 1999; Gonchar and Burkhalter, 2003; Hangya et al., 2014), which provide feedforward inhibition (FFI) to local Pyr cells (Dong et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating this circuit motif.

claim: Feedforward inhibition is capable of regulating the inhibition/excitation balance and influencing gain, integration window, and temporal precision of inputs.
source: FFI is a common functional motif throughout the brain, capable of regulating the I/E balance and thereby influencing the gain, the integration window, and the temporal precision of inputs (Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Atallah et al., 2012; Gabernet et al., 2005; Cardin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: Feedforward input to pyramidal cells is more strongly counterbalanced by inhibition than feedback input.
source: In fact, our studies in mouse visual cortex have shown that FF input to Pyr cells is more strongly counterbalanced by inhibition than FB input, suggesting pathway-specific differences in the gain and dynamic range of recurrent excitation involved in cortical computations (Yang et al., 2013; Atallah et al., 2012; Okun and Lampl, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors and others.

claim: Higher relative inhibition in feedforward than in feedback pathways is part of a more general rule of cortico-cortical communication.
source: Here, we demonstrate that higher relative inhibition in FF than in FB pathways is part of a more general rule of cortico-cortical communication.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by data across multiple pathways.

claim: Pyramidal cells in higher areas have a higher density of dendritic spines than those in lower areas in primates.
source: Pertinently, Pyr cells in higher areas have been shown to have a higher density of dendritic spines than those in lower areas in both primates (Elston, 2003) and rodents (Elston et al., 2006), indicating that Pyr neurons in higher areas must integrate a larger number of excitatory inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous anatomical study in primates.

claim: Pyramidal cells in higher areas have a higher density of dendritic spines than those in lower areas in rodents.
source: Pertinently, Pyr cells in higher areas have been shown to have a higher density of dendritic spines than those in lower areas in both primates (Elston, 2003) and rodents (Elston et al., 2006), indicating that Pyr neurons in higher areas must integrate a larger number of excitatory inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous anatomical study in rodents.

claim: PV neurons normalize cortical activity by inhibiting pyramidal cells by a level proportional to the latter's excitation, thus controlling their gain.
source: In particular, PV neurons normalize cortical activity by inhibiting Pyr cells by a level that is proportional to the latter's excitation, thus controlling their gain (Atallah et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on gain control mechanisms.

claim: Strong activation of PV neurons may narrow the window for effective excitation and result in high frequency gamma-band synchronization found in feedforward signaling.
source: Strong activation of PV neurons may narrow the window for effective excitation and result in high frequency gamma-band synchronization of activity found in FF signaling (Gabernet et al., 2005; Cardin et al., 2009; Bastos et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous studies on oscillations.

claim: In feedback pathways, excitation is weakly counterbalanced by inhibition, which may broaden the window for synaptic integration and result in slower synchronization frequencies.
source: In contrast, in FB pathways excitation is weakly counterbalanced by inhibition, which may broaden the window for synaptic integration and result in slower synchronization frequencies found in FB communications (Bastos et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citation to a previous study on oscillations.

claim: Variation in inhibition/excitation balance through differential recruitment of PV and pyramidal neurons is a key feature of distributed hierarchical processing.
source: Thus, variation in I/E balance, through the differential recruitment of PV and Pyr neurons in different cortical pathways, is a key feature of distributed hierarchical processing.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings and their interpretation.

claim: Feedforward projections tend to avoid L1 across different mammalian species.
source: Despite these differences, a consistent observation among different species is a tendency for FF projections to avoid L1 and the selective targeting of L1 by FB pathways (Coogan and Burkhalter, 1993; Rockland and Virga, 1989; Henry et al., 1991; Cauller, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies in multiple species.

claim: Feedback pathways selectively target L1 across different mammalian species.
source: Despite these differences, a consistent observation among different species is a tendency for FF projections to avoid L1 and the selective targeting of L1 by FB pathways (Coogan and Burkhalter, 1993; Rockland and Virga, 1989; Henry et al., 1991; Cauller, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies in multiple species.

claim: The hierarchical ordering of V1, LM and PM based on average density ratios is consistent with the ordering based on increasing receptive field sizes.
source: In this reference frame, V1, LM and PM constitute a clear hierarchy, which broadly matches that of rat visual cortex (Coogan and Burkhalter, 1993) and is consistent with the increasing size of receptive fields (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous physiological study on receptive field properties.

claim: Interareal inputs to L5 may be driving pyramidal cells, similar to thalamocortical input.
source: The laminar difference may indicate that, similar to thalamocortical input (Constantinople and Bruno, 2013), interareal inputs to L5 are driving Pyr cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on analogy to thalamocortical circuits, supported by citation.

claim: Interareal communication may occur through cortico-thalamo-cortical loops.
source: This may enable interareal communication through cortico-thalamo-cortical loops (Guillery and Sherman, 2002) as well as with subcortical motor targets, thereby linking perception and action (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous studies on thalamic circuits.

claim: VIP-expressing interneurons are an important target of long-range and neuromodulatory inputs.
source: For instance, neocortical GABAergic interneurons that express vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) are thought to be an important target of long-range and neuromodulatory inputs (Fu et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014), and in turn, primarily inhibit other interneurons leading to disinhibition of cortical Pyr cells (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Pi et al., 2013; Karnani et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on VIP interneuron circuits.

claim: VIP interneurons primarily inhibit other interneurons, leading to disinhibition of cortical pyramidal cells.
source: For instance, neocortical GABAergic interneurons that express vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) are thought to be an important target of long-range and neuromodulatory inputs (Fu et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014), and in turn, primarily inhibit other interneurons leading to disinhibition of cortical Pyr cells (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Pi et al., 2013; Karnani et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on VIP interneuron connectivity.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing interneurons make extensive inhibitory contacts with local pyramidal cells.
source: Somatostatin (SOM)-expressing interneurons, which include Martinotti cells, make extensive inhibitory contacts with local Pyr cells, and can consequently mediate disynaptic inhibition between neighboring Pyr cells (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Silberberg and Markram, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on SOM interneuron connectivity.

claim: SOM neurons provide inhibitory inputs to other interneurons, including PV cells.
source: SOM neurons have also been shown to provide inhibitory inputs to other interneurons, including PV cells, suggesting a role in the disinhibition of Pyr cells as well (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on interneuron connectivity.

claim: Glutamate release can induce suppression of GABA release by activating presynaptic metabotropic receptors.
source: By activating pre- and postsynaptic metabotropic receptors in various neocortical circuits, glutamate release can induce suppression of GABA release and inhibition of L4 neurons, respectively (Liu et al., 2014; Lee and Sherman, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on metabotropic receptor function.

claim: Glutamate can induce inhibition of L4 neurons by activating postsynaptic metabotropic receptors.
source: By activating pre- and postsynaptic metabotropic receptors in various neocortical circuits, glutamate release can induce suppression of GABA release and inhibition of L4 neurons, respectively (Liu et al., 2014; Lee and Sherman, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on metabotropic receptor function.

claim: Multiple, partially overlapping sources of inhibition may be differentially recruited depending on context.
source: Thus, multiple, partially overlapping (Gonchar et al., 2007) sources of inhibition may be differentially recruited depending on context, providing a multilayered control of cortical function (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Pakan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous studies on interneuron diversity.

claim: Excitation ascending across multiple hierarchical levels is gradually adjusted to keep the dynamic range of L2/3 pyramidal cell firing constant.
source: Our findings argue that excitation ascending across multiple hierarchical levels is gradually adjusted to keep the dynamic range of L2/3 Pyr cell firing constant and compensate for the increased density of synaptic input to Pyr cells in higher cortical areas (Elston, 2003).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the findings, combining experimental data with citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: Lower inhibition/excitation levels in feedback pathways would broaden the window of opportunity for spikes to be integrated.
source: On the other hand, lower I/E levels in FB pathways would broaden the 'window of opportunity' for spikes to be integrated and trigger an output in the postsynaptic cell (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011), suggesting that FB signals originating in association cortex require less gain control than FF signals.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citation to a previous theoretical study.

claim: Feedback pathways are well-placed to prime pyramidal cells to selectively respond to feedforward input in a context-dependent manner.
source: Rather, by broadly modulating the excitability of neurons in lower areas (such as by targeting the primary dendrites of Pyr cells in L1/2), FB pathways are well-placed to prime Pyr cells to selectively respond to FF input in a context-dependent manner (Larkum, 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citation to a previous study on dendritic integration.

claim: Sparse coding in L2/3 pyramidal cells and dense excitation in L5 pyramidal cells allow for distinct computational strategies.
source: This provides a putative mechanism for the previously observed sparse coding in L2/3 Pyr cells and dense excitation in intrinsically burst-spiking L5 Pyr cells, allowing for distinct computational strategies within individual neurons depending on their postsynaptic targets (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013; Hefti and Smith, 2000; Schubert et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to previous studies on coding strategies.

claim: Interareal inputs to L5 may enable interareal communication through cortico-thalamo-cortical loops and with subcortical motor targets.
source: This may enable interareal communication through cortico-thalamo-cortical loops (Guillery and Sherman, 2002) as well as with subcortical motor targets, thereby linking perception and action (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Signals sent to deeper parts of the brain from more peripheral areas are more potently controlled by inhibition than pathways originating in higher areas.
source: Our observation that L2/3 PV cells are recruited most strongly by pathways transmitting signals from V1 to higher cortical areas imply that signals sent to deeper parts of the brain from more peripheral areas are more potently controlled by inhibition than pathways originating in higher areas.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: High levels of inhibition may be crucial for pyramidal cells to efficiently integrate excitatory input from a large number of areas.
source: Such a high level of inhibition may be crucial in order for Pyr cells to efficiently integrate excitatory input from a large number of areas.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: Interareal inhibitory circuits make pyramidal cells coincidence-detectors, leading to reduction of noise levels and preservation of temporal precision.
source: Such an interareal inhibitory circuit would make Pyr cells coincidence-detectors (Gabernet et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001), leading to a reduction of noise levels and the preservation of temporal precision in the target area (Bruno, 2011; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous studies on coincidence detection.

claim: Coincidence-detection helps achieve a wide dynamic range by allowing only a fraction of excitatory inputs to summate and evoke a spike response.
source: Coincidence-detection has also been proposed to help achieve a wide dynamic range by allowing only a fraction of excitatory inputs to summate and evoke a spike response (Shadlen and Newsome, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous theoretical study.
